periods.name: Xia dynasty
periods.note: The first dynasty of the old Chinese histories. Whether it was real is still argued; the bronze-age city at Erlitou may have been its capital.

periods.name: Shang dynasty
periods.note: Kings at Anyang put questions to their ancestors on oracle bones, the oldest Chinese writing, and cast great ritual bronzes.

periods.name: Western Zhou
periods.note: The Zhou overthrew the Shang, claiming the Mandate of Heaven, and ruled through lords of their own clan from near Xi'an.

periods.name: Spring and Autumn period
periods.note: With the Zhou kings weak in Luoyang, their lords became rival states. Confucius taught in the small state of Lu.

periods.name: Warring States
periods.note: Seven kingdoms fought with mass armies of iron while thinkers argued how to rule: Mencius, the Daoists, the Legalists.

periods.name: Qin dynasty
periods.note: Qin Shi Huang united China in 221 BC, made one script, one coinage and one length of axle, and was buried with an army of clay.

periods.name: Han dynasty
periods.note: Four centuries that gave the Han Chinese their name: Confucian officials, paper and the Silk Road. Wang Mang's Xin dynasty broke it in two (AD 9 to 23).

periods.name: Three Kingdoms
periods.note: Wei, Shu and Wu fought over the fallen Han, the age retold in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

periods.name: Jin dynasty
periods.note: The Jin reunited China in 280 but lost the north in 316 to peoples of the steppe, the Sixteen Kingdoms; the Eastern Jin held the south from Nanjing.

periods.name: Northern and Southern dynasties
periods.note: Buddhism spread while northern dynasties founded by the Xianbei faced southern ones ruled from Nanjing.

periods.name: Sui dynasty
periods.note: Reunited China in 589 and dug the Grand Canal between the Yellow River and the Yangtze, then fell after failed wars in Korea.

periods.name: Tang dynasty
periods.note: A golden age of poetry (Li Bai, Du Fu) and an open, cosmopolitan capital at Chang'an. Wu Zetian ruled as emperor in her own name.

periods.name: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms
periods.note: Five short-lived dynasties followed each other in the north while ten kingdoms divided the south.

periods.name: Song dynasty
periods.note: Printing, gunpowder, the compass and paper money, and cities of a million people. The Liao, Western Xia and Jin held the north.

periods.name: Yuan dynasty
periods.note: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, ruled China from Beijing (Khanbaliq) as emperor of a Mongol dynasty.

periods.name: Ming dynasty
periods.note: Zheng He's treasure fleets sailed to Africa, the Forbidden City was built and the Great Wall took its brick form.

periods.name: Qing dynasty
periods.note: Manchu emperors doubled China's size. In the 1800s the Opium Wars and the Taiping rebellion broke its strength.

periods.name: Republic of China
periods.note: Sun Yat-sen's republic fell to warlords; Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists then fought the Communists and, from 1937, Japan.

periods.name: People's Republic of China
periods.note: Mao Zedong's People's Republic, then from 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms that made China the workshop of the world.

periods.name: Jōmon period
periods.note: Hunters, fishers and gatherers who made some of the oldest pottery in the world, marked with cord patterns (jōmon).

periods.name: Yayoi period
periods.note: Rice farming, bronze and iron came over from Korea; Chinese records tell of Queen Himiko of Yamatai.

periods.name: Kofun period
periods.note: Chiefs were buried in great keyhole-shaped mounds as the Yamato clan rose to rule from the Nara plain.

periods.name: Asuka period
periods.note: Buddhism arrived from Korea; Prince Shōtoku wrote the first constitution and the court took the name Nihon.

periods.name: Nara period
periods.note: A capital on the Chinese plan at Nara, the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji and the first histories, the Kojiki and Nihon shoki.

periods.name: Heian period
periods.note: The court at Kyoto, run by the Fujiwara regents, wrote The Tale of Genji while warrior clans grew in the provinces.

periods.name: Kamakura period
periods.note: Minamoto no Yoritomo became the first shogun; samurai rule from Kamakura beat back two Mongol invasions.

periods.name: Muromachi period
periods.note: The Ashikaga shoguns in Kyoto: Zen gardens, nō theatre and the tea ceremony, then from 1467 a century of civil war.

periods.name: Azuchi–Momoyama period
periods.note: Oda Nobunaga and then Toyotomi Hideyoshi united Japan with guns brought by the Portuguese, and Hideyoshi invaded Korea.

periods.name: Edo period
periods.note: Two and a half centuries of peace under the Tokugawa shoguns in Edo (Tokyo), with Japan closed to most of the world.

periods.name: Meiji era
periods.note: The emperor was restored and Japan made itself a modern industrial power, beating China in 1895 and Russia in 1905.

periods.name: Taishō era
periods.note: A brief time of party government and mass culture, with Japan among the victors of the First World War.

periods.name: Shōwa era
periods.note: Militarism and the Pacific War, defeat and the atomic bombs in 1945, American occupation, then the economic miracle.

periods.name: Heisei era
periods.note: The bubble burst into the "lost decades"; the 2011 earthquake and tsunami struck the northeast.

periods.name: Reiwa era
periods.note: The reign of Emperor Naruhito.

periods.name: Gojoseon
periods.note: By tradition founded by Dangun in 2333 BC; in the records it is a kingdom of the north, ended by a Han Chinese invasion in 108 BC.

periods.name: Proto–Three Kingdoms
periods.note: Han commanderies in the north beside Buyeo, Okjeo and the Samhan confederacies of the south.

periods.name: Three Kingdoms
periods.note: Goguryeo in the north, Baekje in the southwest and Silla in the southeast, until Silla allied with Tang China and won.

periods.name: Unified Silla and Balhae
periods.note: Silla ruled the peninsula from Gyeongju, building Bulguksa temple, while Balhae held the old Goguryeo lands to the north.

periods.name: Goryeo
periods.note: The dynasty that gave Korea its name in the west: celadon pottery, the Tripitaka Koreana and metal movable type. It bowed to the Mongols from 1270.

periods.name: Joseon
periods.note: A Confucian kingdom ruled from Seoul. King Sejong created the hangul alphabet; Admiral Yi's turtle ships beat back Japan in the 1590s.

periods.name: Korean Empire
periods.note: Joseon renamed itself an empire to stand equal to China and Japan, but Japan made it a protectorate in 1905.

periods.name: Japanese rule
periods.note: Korea was annexed by Japan; its people were made to take Japanese names and many were forced to work for the war.

periods.name: Division and the Korean War
periods.note: Split at the 38th parallel between Soviet and American forces; North Korea invaded the South in 1950.

periods.name: North and South Korea
periods.note: The communist North under the Kim family and the South, poor at first, then rich and, from 1987, democratic.

periods.name: Xiongnu
periods.note: The first great empire of the steppe, founded by Modu Chanyu; the Han dynasty paid it tribute and built walls against it.

periods.name: Xianbei
periods.note: The Xianbei took the steppe from the Xiongnu; some of their clans later founded dynasties in northern China.

periods.name: Rouran Khaganate
periods.note: The Rouran were the first to call their ruler khagan; their Turkic blacksmith subjects rose against them.

periods.name: Turkic Khaganates
periods.note: The Göktürks ruled from Manchuria to the Black Sea and left the Orkhon inscriptions, the oldest Turkic writing.

periods.name: Uyghur Khaganate
periods.note: The Uyghurs ruled from their walled capital Ordu-Baliq, saved the Tang from rebellion and took up the Manichaean faith.

periods.name: Kyrgyz and Khitan rule
periods.note: The Yenisei Kyrgyz broke the Uyghurs; then the Khitan Liao dynasty of northern China held the steppe.

periods.name: Mongol tribes
periods.note: Rival clans and peoples, the Mongols, Tatars, Keraites and Naimans, until Temüjin united them all.

periods.name: Mongol Empire
periods.note: Genghis Khan and his heirs built the largest land empire ever, from Korea to Hungary; Kublai moved its capital to Beijing.

periods.name: Northern Yuan
periods.note: Driven out of China, the Mongols fought each other and the Ming; Altan Khan brought Tibetan Buddhism back to Mongolia.

periods.name: Qing rule
periods.note: The Khalkha Mongols submitted to the Manchu Qing emperor Kangxi, and Mongolia was ruled from Beijing for two centuries.

periods.name: Bogd Khanate
periods.note: When the Qing fell, Mongolia declared independence under the Bogd Khan, its highest Buddhist lama.

periods.name: Mongolian People's Republic
periods.note: The world's second communist state, close to the Soviet Union, which helped it beat Japan at Khalkhin Gol in 1939.

periods.name: Mongolia
periods.note: A peaceful revolution in 1990 brought democracy and a market economy.

periods.name: Zhangzhung and early Tibet
periods.note: The kingdom of Zhangzhung around Mount Kailash, home of the Bon faith, and the valley chiefs of central Tibet.

periods.name: Tibetan Empire
periods.note: Songtsen Gampo united the plateau and brought Buddhism; Tibet took Chang'an itself for a few days in 763.

periods.name: Era of Fragmentation
periods.note: The empire broke apart; Buddhism came back in a second spread from India, with Atiśa and the great translators.

periods.name: Mongol rule
periods.note: The lamas of Sakya ruled Tibet for the Mongol khans, after Kublai Khan made Phagpa his preceptor.

periods.name: Phagmodrupa and Tsangpa kings
periods.note: Native dynasties ruled while Tsongkhapa founded the Gelug school; Altan Khan gave its leader the title Dalai Lama.

periods.name: Ganden Phodrang
periods.note: The fifth Dalai Lama ruled Tibet with Mongol support and began the Potala Palace in Lhasa.

periods.name: Qing protectorate
periods.note: Qing armies installed a government in Lhasa with two Manchu residents (ambans) watching over it.

periods.name: Independent Tibet
periods.note: After the Qing fell, the thirteenth Dalai Lama ruled Tibet as an independent country in all but recognition.

periods.name: Part of the People's Republic of China
periods.note: The People's Liberation Army entered Tibet in 1950; after the 1959 uprising the fourteenth Dalai Lama fled to India.

periods.name: Indigenous Taiwan
periods.note: Austronesian peoples, whose languages spread from Taiwan across the Pacific and the Indian Ocean as far as Madagascar.

periods.name: Dutch and Spanish Formosa
periods.note: The Dutch East India Company held Fort Zeelandia in the south, the Spanish a fort in the north until 1642.

periods.name: Kingdom of Tungning
periods.note: Koxinga, a Ming loyalist, drove out the Dutch, and his family ruled Taiwan until the Qing took it.

periods.name: Qing Taiwan
periods.note: Han Chinese settlers from Fujian and Guangdong farmed the west of the island, while the mountains stayed indigenous.

periods.name: Japanese Taiwan
periods.note: Ceded to Japan after the war of 1894 to 1895, Taiwan was built up as a model colony of railways, rice and sugar.

periods.name: Republic of China
periods.note: Chiang Kai-shek's government retreated here in 1949; after decades of martial law Taiwan became a democracy.

periods.name: Văn Lang and Âu Lạc
periods.note: The Hùng kings and the bronze drums of the Đông Sơn culture in the Red River delta.

periods.name: Chinese rule
periods.note: A thousand years under Nanyue and the Chinese dynasties, broken by risings such as the Trưng sisters' in AD 40.

periods.name: Ngô, Đinh and Early Lê
periods.note: Ngô Quyền beat the Southern Han fleet on the Bạch Đằng River in 938 and Vietnam was free.

periods.name: Lý dynasty
periods.note: The Lý moved the capital to Thăng Long (Hanoi) and founded the Temple of Literature.

periods.name: Trần dynasty
periods.note: Trần Hưng Đạo drove back three Mongol invasions, the last again on the Bạch Đằng River.

periods.name: Hồ dynasty and Ming rule
periods.note: The Ming invaded in 1407 and ruled for twenty years.

periods.name: Later Lê dynasty
periods.note: Lê Lợi drove out the Ming. In later centuries the Lê were puppets of the Trịnh lords in the north and the Nguyễn in the south.

periods.name: Tây Sơn dynasty
periods.note: Three brothers from Tây Sơn overthrew both lords and routed a Qing army at Đống Đa in 1789.

periods.name: Nguyễn dynasty
periods.note: Gia Long united the whole country from the citadel of Huế and named it Việt Nam.

periods.name: French Indochina
periods.note: France ruled the north (Tonkin), the centre (Annam) and the south (Cochinchina), with Cambodia and Laos.

periods.name: Wars of independence and division
periods.note: Hồ Chí Minh declared independence in 1945; war with France and then America, and division from 1954 to 1975.

periods.name: Socialist Republic of Vietnam
periods.note: Reunited under the Communist Party, which opened the economy with the Đổi Mới reforms of 1986.

periods.name: Funan
periods.note: A trading kingdom of the Mekong delta whose port of Óc Eo linked India and China.

periods.name: Chenla
periods.note: A Khmer kingdom of the middle Mekong that took over Funan and later split into "land" and "water" Chenla.

periods.name: Khmer Empire
periods.note: Jayavarman II declared himself a god-king in 802; his heirs built Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom.

periods.name: Post-Angkor period
periods.note: After Ayutthaya sacked Angkor the kings moved south to Phnom Penh, squeezed between Siam and Vietnam.

periods.name: French protectorate
periods.note: King Norodom accepted French protection to save his country from its neighbours.

periods.name: Kingdom and Khmer Republic
periods.note: Independent under Norodom Sihanouk, then drawn into the Vietnam War and civil war.

periods.name: Khmer Rouge
periods.note: Pol Pot emptied the cities; about a quarter of Cambodians died of killing, hunger and forced labour.

periods.name: Modern Cambodia
periods.note: Vietnamese occupation, UN-run elections in 1993 and the return of the monarchy.

periods.name: Dvaravati
periods.note: Mon Buddhist city-states of the Chao Phraya basin, with the Khmer ruling much of the land from Angkor.

periods.name: Sukhothai Kingdom
periods.note: The first Thai kingdom; King Ram Khamhaeng is said to have made the Thai script.

periods.name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
periods.note: A river capital that traded with China, Japan, Persia and Europe, until Burma burned it in 1767.

periods.name: Thonburi Kingdom
periods.note: General Taksin drove out the Burmese and ruled from Thonburi.

periods.name: Rattanakosin Kingdom (Siam)
periods.note: The Chakri kings in Bangkok; Mongkut and Chulalongkorn kept Siam the only country of the region never colonised.

periods.name: Constitutional monarchy
periods.note: A revolution in 1932 limited the king's power; Siam became Thailand in 1939, ruled by turns by generals and parliaments.

periods.name: Pyu city-states
periods.note: Walled Buddhist cities of the Pyu people in the dry zone of the Irrawaddy.

periods.name: Pagan Kingdom
periods.note: The first Burmese empire; its kings and people built more than ten thousand temples on the plain of Bagan.

periods.name: Ava, Hanthawaddy and the Shan states
periods.note: After the Mongol invasions the land split between Ava in the north and the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy in the south.

periods.name: Toungoo dynasty
periods.note: Bayinnaung built the largest empire in Southeast Asian history, taking Ayutthaya in 1564.

periods.name: Konbaung dynasty
periods.note: Alaungpaya reunited Burma; his heirs sacked Ayutthaya, then lost three wars to the British.

periods.name: British Burma
periods.note: Ruled as a province of British India until 1937; fought over between Japan and the Allies in the Second World War.

periods.name: Independent Myanmar
periods.note: Independent in 1948, then under army rule from 1962; Aung San Suu Kyi's brief democracy ended in a coup in 2021.

periods.name: Early kingdoms
periods.note: Hindu and Buddhist kingdoms traded across the straits: Kutai in Borneo and Tarumanagara in Java.

periods.name: Srivijaya and Mataram
periods.note: Srivijaya at Palembang ruled the sea lanes, while the Sailendra kings of Java built Borobudur and Prambanan.

periods.name: Singhasari and Majapahit
periods.note: Javanese empires that beat off Kublai Khan; under its minister Gajah Mada, Majapahit ruled much of the archipelago.

periods.name: Islamic sultanates
periods.note: Islam spread through the ports: Demak, Aceh, Banten and Mataram, while the Dutch East India Company took the spice trade.

periods.name: Dutch East Indies
periods.note: The Dutch state took over from the bankrupt company and ruled the islands for their coffee, sugar and oil.

periods.name: Japanese occupation and revolution
periods.note: Japan occupied the islands; Sukarno declared independence in 1945 and the Dutch recognised it in 1949.

periods.name: Republic of Indonesia
periods.note: Sukarno, then Suharto's New Order from 1965 to 1998, then democracy.

periods.name: Barangays and sultanates
periods.note: Villages and chiefdoms (barangays), the kingdoms of Tondo and Cebu and the sultanate of Sulu.

periods.name: Spanish Philippines
periods.note: Spain ruled from Manila, the end of the galleon route to Acapulco, and made the islands Catholic.

periods.name: American rule
periods.note: The United States took the islands from Spain and fought a war against the new Philippine Republic.

periods.name: Republic of the Philippines
periods.note: Independent in 1946; Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law until the People Power revolution of 1986.

periods.name: Early Malay kingdoms
periods.note: Ports such as Kedah and Langkasuka, under the shadow of Srivijaya and then Majapahit.

periods.name: Malacca Sultanate
periods.note: Malacca grew into the great port of the straits and spread Islam along them.

periods.name: Portuguese and Dutch Malacca
periods.note: The Portuguese and then the Dutch held Malacca, while sultanates such as Johor ruled the rest.

periods.name: British Malaya
periods.note: The Straits Settlements and the protected Malay states, rich in tin and rubber.

periods.name: Malaysia
periods.note: Independent as Malaya in 1957, joined with Sabah, Sarawak and for a while Singapore as Malaysia in 1963.
